Three or four months passed, and by then winter was well underway. I had gone to school most days and learned a little spelling, reading, and writing. I could recite the multiplication table up to six times seven is thirty-five, and I doubt I could go any farther if I lived forever. Anyway, I don’t have much use for mathematics.

I hated school at first, but eventually I learned to put up with it. Whenever I got especially sick of it, I skipped a day. The beating I got the next morning did me good and cheered me up. The longer I went, the easier school became. I was getting used to the widow’s habits too, and they didn’t bother me so much. Living indoors and sleeping in a bed usually made me feel terribly trapped. Before the cold weather, though, I sometimes slipped out to sleep in the woods, which gave me a break. I still liked my old life best, but I was starting to like the new one a little. The widow said I was making slow, steady progress and doing very well. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning I accidentally tipped over the salt dish at breakfast. I reached for some salt as quickly as possible, meaning to throw it over my left shoulder and prevent bad luck. But Miss Watson stopped me before I could. “Take your hands away, Huckleberry,” she said. “You’re always making such a mess!” The widow defended me, but I knew perfectly well that wouldn’t protect me from the bad luck. After breakfast I headed outside, nervous and worried, wondering where trouble would catch me and what it would be. There are ways to prevent certain kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of them. So I didn’t try anything. I just wandered along, feeling miserable and keeping my eyes open.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the steps that crossed the high wooden fence. An inch of fresh snow covered the ground, and I spotted someone’s footprints. They led up from the quarry, stopped around the fence steps for a while, then continued around the garden fence. It was strange that whoever made them hadn’t come in after waiting there so long. I couldn’t work it out. Something about it was very odd. I was about to follow the tracks around the fence, but first I bent down to examine them.

Poor Jack was later killed in a duel with Lord Canterville on Wandsworth Common, and before the year ended Lady Barbara died of heartbreak at Tunbridge Wells; thus, in every respect, the affair had proved a great success. The ‘make-up,’ however, was extraordinarily troublesome—if I may apply such a theatrical phrase to one of the supreme mysteries of the supernatural, or, in more scientific language, the higher-natural realm—and his preparations occupied a full three hours. When everything was finally arranged, he was highly pleased with his looks. The large leather riding-boots belonging to the costume were somewhat too big, and he had located only one of the pair of horse-pistols; nevertheless, he felt satisfied on the whole. At a quarter after one he slipped through the wainscoting and stole along the corridor. Arriving at the twins’ room, which, I should explain, was known as the Blue Bed Chamber from the colour of its curtains, he found its door slightly open. Desiring a striking entrance, he threw it wide. A heavy jug of water immediately dropped upon him, drenching him through and missing his left shoulder by scarcely two inches. Simultaneously, suppressed shrieks of laughter came from the four-poster. So violently were his nerves shaken that he rushed back to his room at his utmost speed, and next day he was confined there by a bad cold. His sole consolation in the entire business was that he had left his head behind; had he brought it, the results might have been exceedingly grave.

He now abandoned any expectation of frightening this uncivil American household. Usually he was content to steal through the passages in list slippers, wearing a heavy red scarf about his neck against draughts and carrying a little arquebuse against attacks by the twins. The last blow befell him on September 19th. He had descended to the great entrance-hall, confident that he would at least be undisturbed there, and was entertaining himself with sarcastic observations on the large Saroni photographs of the United States Minister and his wife that now replaced the Canterville family portraits. His attire was simple but tidy: a long shroud flecked with graveyard mould. A band of yellow linen held up his jaw, and he bore a small lantern and a sexton’s spade.

“This marriage is exactly right. I didn’t believe that at first, but I admit it now. The gods created Sibyl Vane for you. Without her, you would never have been complete.”

“Thank you, Basil,” Dorian Gray replied, squeezing his hand. “I knew you would understand. Harry’s cynicism frightens me. But the orchestra is starting. It’s dreadful, though it only goes on for about five minutes. Then the curtain rises, and you’ll see the girl I intend to give my whole life to, the girl who already has everything good in me.”

Fifteen minutes later, Sibyl Vane walked onto the stage amid an extraordinary roar of applause. Yes, she was undeniably beautiful—one of the most beautiful creatures Lord Henry had ever seen. Her shy grace and startled eyes reminded him of a fawn. As she glanced at the crowded, enthusiastic audience, a delicate blush touched her cheeks, like a rose reflected in a silver mirror. She took a few steps backward, and her lips seemed to shake. Basil Hallward jumped up and began clapping. Dorian Gray remained motionless, staring at her as if dreaming. Looking through his opera glasses, Lord Henry murmured, “Delightful! Delightful!”

The setting was the hall in Capulet’s house. Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had entered with Mercutio and his other friends. The band, such as it was, played a few bars, and the dancing began. Among the awkward, poorly dressed actors, Sibyl Vane moved as though she belonged to a more beautiful world. As she danced, her body swayed like a plant in water. Her throat had the curves of a white lily; her hands looked carved from cool ivory.

Yet she seemed strangely lifeless. No happiness showed when she looked at Romeo. Her few lines—

“Good pilgrim, you are too harsh on your hand, which shows such courteous devotion. Saints have hands for pilgrims to touch, and joining palms is the holy pilgrim’s kiss”—

and the short exchange that followed sounded completely artificial. Her voice was exquisite, but her tone was entirely wrong. Its emotional coloring did not fit. It drained the poetry of life and made the passion seem false.

Dorian Gray turned pale as he watched. He felt bewildered and anxious. Neither friend dared speak to him. To both of them, she seemed utterly unable to act.
